attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post. He states this as his own finding.

semantics.note: Faithful, and keeps 'for the most part', 'it appears' and 'around'. 'It appears' frames a research conclusion; it is not a probability hedge of the kind the policy lists. The part about his own search can't be checked; the 18-month typical duration can.

contract.note: Reading it as an approximate typical build time for modest facilities like his examples is ordinary and fair. Treating JLL's 'build time' as groundbreaking-to-opening is an interpretation, but a reasonable one.

evidence.note: JLL 2026 outlook, public January 2026: average global build time for a 50 MW data center is 18 months. That is a facility size comparable to several of his examples. Independent industry research.

reviews.rationale: The checkable part, that a modest data center typically takes around 18 months from groundbreaking to opening, matches JLL's contemporaneous benchmark of 18 months for a 50 MW facility. The packet lists no counterevidence. The claim that he found only a few completed facilities is about his own search and is not scored.

attribution.note: Zitron's own unhedged statement in his own post.

semantics.note: 'As of May 2026, nobody has built a 1GW campus' matches the statement and its 'yet', including his note that such a data center is usually a multi-building campus.

contract.note: Reading 'built' as at least 1,000 MW commissioned and operating at publication fits the context. Whether the threshold is total facility power or IT power is the evaluator's choice and could decide the result: New Carlisle is near the line.

evidence.note: Epoch estimates 910 MW of IT power operating at New Carlisle by March 2026, inferred from satellite imagery. That is IT power, not total facility power, and the date is an estimate, so it neither establishes nor excludes 1 GW of facility power.
Epoch estimates about 490 MW of IT power at Colossus 2 as of April 2026. This is a partial buildout recorded before the target interval and is below the threshold.

reviews.rationale: The claim is a global negative, and the packet has no worldwide inventory of operating capacity. New Carlisle's estimated 910 MW of IT power might or might not mean 1 GW or more of facility power. That depends on a conversion and commissioning dates the packet doesn't settle. The other campus checked was below the threshold. The evidence neither confirms nor refutes the claim.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: Faithful. 'Shows' stands in for 'a clear sign', and the deal is offered as an indicator. The testable content is the claim that most AI data centers don't get finished and that finished ones take two to three years.

contract.note: The contract's choices are reasonable but are the evaluator's, not the speaker's: the Q1 2026 period, 'mostly' meaning a majority of overdue projects, and 24–36 months from construction start to use. 'Smaller builds' has no size threshold.

evidence.note: Sightline says typical build timelines are 12–18 months for projects over 50MW, and gives figures on slippage and delays. The timeline figure is an analyst's benchmark, not a measured cohort of completed projects, and the delay figures are forward-looking, so it doesn't settle either part. It is material counterevidence on build times.
Epoch's methodology note covers how operational dates are inferred for large US campuses. It does not measure completion rates or build times for smaller facilities.
Anthropic's own announcement confirms the Colossus 1 agreement. It says nothing about industry completion rates.

reviews.rationale: No representative cohort in the packet establishes that most AI projects went unfinished, or what typical build times are for smaller facilities. Sightline's 12–18 month benchmark points against the two-to-three-year figure, but it is not measured completion data. The delay statistics suggest a minority of projects slipping, not a majority, and are mostly forward-looking. The claim is unresolved on this packet.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: Faithful. It keeps 'based on my research', 'a piece' and 'since 2023'. Taken literally, the second part reports his own search; in context it asserts that hyperscalers added only limited capacity.

contract.note: Testing 'no compelling evidence' against public pre-publication disclosures is a fair plain reading. Whether formal investor disclosures count as compelling is a judgment the speaker contests. The contract allows operator disclosures as sources.

evidence.note: AWS says it deployed new liquid-cooling units in production data centers for dense AI chips. This supports the retrofit part. It is a company disclosure and shows one provider at limited scale.
Microsoft's annual report, October 2025: over two gigawatts of new capacity added that year. This is a company disclosure of additions already made.
Amazon's Q3 2025 report: AWS added 3.8 GW of power capacity in the prior 12 months. This is a company disclosure of additions already made.
Microsoft's FY26 Q3 remarks, public April 29, 2026: another gigawatt added in the quarter. Only the backward-looking figure is used.

reviews.rationale: The retrofit part holds: AWS and Microsoft disclosures describe adapting existing facilities for AI cooling. The capacity part is contradicted. Microsoft and Amazon each publicly reported gigawatt-scale additions before publication, well above a few hundred megawatts each. These are company disclosures, not independent measurements, but they are formal investor statements of realized additions.
